impact_facts: A disproportionate concentration: The Mediterranean Sea represents only 1% of the world's ocean surface, yet it concentrates 7% of all microplastics on the planet.

The absurdity of single-use: It takes about 1 second to manufacture a plastic bag and its average use lasts only 20 minutes, yet it will take more than a century to degrade in the natural environment.
Millennial persistence: While a cigarette butt takes about 10 years to degrade at sea, a plastic fishing line can take up to 600 years to disappear.
The global scale: An estimated 5.25 trillion plastic particles are currently floating on the ocean surface, equivalent to a weight of nearly 269,000 tonnes.

Omnipresence in the Mediterranean: The average plastic density in the Mediterranean (1 object every 4 m²) is comparable to that of the five major subtropical oceanic gyres, often called 'plastic continents'.

A deadly trap for wildlife: Sea turtles confuse transparent plastics with jellyfish, causing serious injuries or death, while dolphins can die with their jaws blocked by plastic rings they tried to play with.
Massive bird contamination: Over 90% of seabirds have already ingested plastic, and projections indicate that 99% of species will be affected by 2050.
The relentless flow: Coastal populations dump about 8 million tonnes of plastic waste into the oceans each year, a figure that could double in a decade without improved waste management.
The cigarette butt scourge: During the 'Clean Calanques' operation in 2023 alone, more than 70,000 cigarette butts were collected, highlighting massive and concerning local pollution.
Unavoidable pollution: During a vast Mediterranean basin sampling campaign, floating plastic debris was found at 100% of analyzed sites.

editorial.title: The Mediterranean: An ecosystem under threat
editorial.h3: Plastic pollution, threatened species and environmental urgency
editorial.p: Although it represents only 1% of world waters, the Mediterranean Sea concentrates 7% of all microplastics on the planet. As a semi-enclosed sea, its waters take about 90 years to renew — durably trapping waste. In Marseille and worldwide, over 600 marine species are impacted by plastic ingestion or entanglement. Through my images and my freediving commitment in the Calanques, I document this urgency to make the invisible, visible.

faq.a: Projet Sentinelle is the annual flagship operation conducted by Team Oxygen for Mediterranean protection. Throughout the year, monitoring, awareness and spot intervention actions are organized on the Marseille coastline. Each autumn, the initiative becomes intensive: a full week of underwater freediving cleanup in the Calanques of Marseille. Teams work between 0 and 20 meters deep, with daily 5-6 hour sessions in the water. Collected waste — mainly plastics and macro-debris — is brought up, sorted and quantified to document the real state of the seafloor.

faq.q: How much waste has the Projet Sentinelle collected?
faq.a: In 4 editions (2022–2025), Projet Sentinelle and Team Oxygen have collected over 5,724 kg of marine waste: 900 kg on the Blue Coast (2022), 1,357 kg at the Frioul Archipelago (2023), 1,147 kg in the Calanques National Park (2024), and 2,320 kg in the Marseille Roadstead (2025).

faq.q: How to participate in Calanques cleanup missions?
faq.a: To participate in cleanup missions in the Calanques of Marseille, contact Team Oxygen via the Contact page on karimsaari.com or join the community through the 'Lovers of the Calanques' Facebook group. Freediving immersions require technical skills and supervised practice. We primarily need volunteers for land logistics support (sorting, weighing, equipment management, awareness raising) as well as kayakers for surface assistance and zone security.

faq.q: Why is the Mediterranean Sea one of the world's most polluted seas for plastic?
faq.a: The Mediterranean acts as a true 'plastic trap': it's a semi-enclosed sea whose waters take about 90 years to renew, while plastics have a lifespan far exceeding a century. Its coasts are densely populated (150 million inhabitants), maritime traffic is very intense (30% of global traffic), and it faces massive tourist pressure. Although it represents only 1% of the world ocean surface, it concentrates 7% of all microplastics on the planet.

faq.q: How much plastic is dumped in the Mediterranean every day?
faq.a: Between 700 and 1,400 tonnes of plastic are dumped every day in the Mediterranean Sea — equivalent to one or two garbage trucks per hour, or 33,800 plastic bottles thrown into the sea every minute. In total, more than a million tonnes of plastic are already in the Mediterranean basin.

faq.q: Where does this plastic waste come from?
faq.a: About 80% of marine waste comes from land activities. It is transported by rivers (like the Rhône, Po or Nile) acting as conveyor belts, by urban runoff (rain sweeping street waste toward the sea), or is directly abandoned on coastlines. The remaining 20% comes from maritime activities such as fishing, aquaculture and maritime transport.

faq.q: What waste is most commonly found at sea and on beaches?
faq.a: Plastic represents 95% of marine waste in the Mediterranean. Most commonly found objects are food packaging, plastic bottles, caps, bags and fishing equipment. Cigarette butts (whose filters contain plastic) are also a major scourge, constituting a large proportion of waste collected on beaches.

faq.q: How long does plastic waste take to degrade at sea?
faq.a: Plastics barely biodegrade on a human timescale; they persist for hundreds of years. A plastic bag takes between 20 and over 100 years to degrade, a plastic bottle about 450 years, and a fishing line up to 600 years. The 'visual' disappearance of waste is misleading: it merely fragments into millions of microplastics under the effect of sun and waves.

faq.q: What are microplastics and why are they so dangerous?
faq.a: Microplastics are tiny plastic fragments measuring less than 5 millimeters, resulting from the degradation of larger waste. They are particularly dangerous because their size is similar to that of plankton. In the Mediterranean, the ratio of microplastics to zooplankton can reach 1 to 2, leading to massive ingestion by fish and other marine predators. Moreover, they act as sponges, concentrating chemical and toxic pollutants on their surface.

faq.q: Does plastic always float on the water surface?
faq.a: No — what we see at the surface is only the tip of the iceberg. An estimated 94% of plastic entering the Mediterranean Sea ends up sinking and settling on the seafloor. The remaining 6% is split between beaches (5%) and the surface (1%). Once on the seabed, in darkness, cold and lack of oxygen, plastic barely degrades anymore.

faq.q: What is the impact of this pollution on marine fauna?
faq.a: The consequences are catastrophic: over 700 marine species are impacted globally, and all Mediterranean sea turtle species are affected by plastic ingestion. Turtles often confuse plastic bags with jellyfish. Large cetaceans swallow microplastics while filtering water, while many birds, fish and dolphins die from intestinal blockages or from entanglement in abandoned ghost nets.

faq.q: Does marine plastic pollution have consequences for human health?
faq.a: Yes, the human food chain is directly contaminated. By eating seafood (such as fish, mussels or oysters) or even through sea salt, we ingest plastics. Currently, a human ingests about 5 grams of plastics per week — the weight of a credit card. These plastics contain and release chemical additives that often act as endocrine disruptors, promoting various diseases.

faq.q: What is the role of tourism in this pollution?
faq.a: The Mediterranean basin receives more than 200 million tourists per year. This seasonal influx causes a 40% increase in waste production in summer, saturating local waste management infrastructure and leading to the direct abandonment of waste on coastlines.

Environmental photography uses images of landscapes, plants or animals to awaken in the viewer the desire to protect them — particularly in the face of dangers nature faces. In the Mediterranean, it becomes a direct witnessing tool: each image of Marseille's Calanques, their seabed or local fauna is visual evidence of ecological urgency.

faq.q: What equipment do you use for underwater photography in the Calanques?
faq.a: Underwater photography in Marseille's Calanques is mainly practiced in freediving, which imposes very different constraints than scuba diving: no bubbles, no noise, natural proximity to fauna. I use a watertight housing with a wide angle to capture the depth of the seabed and natural Mediterranean light. The exceptional transparency of Calanques water — between 15 and 30 meters visibility — allows images of rare clarity, both for underwater landscapes and for documentation of species like octopuses, groupers and posidonia.

faq.q: Where can I see your underwater photographs of Marseille's Calanques?
faq.a: My underwater photographs of the Calanques are accessible on this site in the gallery dedicated to underwater photography, gathering over 58 shots taken during Projet Sentinelle cleanup missions (2022–2025). You can also find a selection of seascapes and landscapes in the landscape photography gallery, as well as on my 500px profile (karimsaari) where my images accumulate over 800,000 impressions.

missions.cleanup_title: How does seafloor waste collection work in Marseille?
missions.cleanup_p: Each seafloor waste collection operation combines freediving and surface logistics. Freedivers descend between 0 and 20 meters to collect plastics, metals and various waste deposited on Calanques seafloor. Recovered bags are sorted aboard, weighed and sent to appropriate treatment channels. This underwater cleaning method in Marseille allows reaching areas inaccessible to conventional sea collection devices.
missions.pollution_title: What waste threatens the Calanques? Types of marine pollution
missions.pollution_lead: Underwater cleanup missions reveal highly diverse marine pollution — from fragmented plastics to abandoned fishing gear, including bulky items swept in by coastal waterway floods.
missions.fauna_p: Ghost nets continue to capture fish, octopuses and spiny lobsters long after being abandoned — what biologists call 'ghost fishing.' Nylon takes 400 to 600 years to degrade, releasing microplastics that enter the marine food chain. Posidonia seagrass meadows, classified as a priority habitat by the European Union, are smothered under heavy waste that blocks photosynthesis and accelerates their regression.
missions.doc_p: Each piece of waste extracted is weighed, sorted and characterized: rigid plastic, plastic film, metal, glass, textile, rubber. This data feeds partner scientific reports and contributes to mapping marine pollution in the Calanques National Park.
missions.dive_quote: Every dive is an inventory. Every waste brought up, data for science.

photos.passion_quote: Twenty years roaming the Mediterranean, from the Basque Coast to the Calanques — and the conviction that the most beautiful landscapes are never at the end of the world, but at the end of the path you take each morning.
photos.learning_p1: It all started with a film camera and summers in the high mountains. As a teenager, I spent every summer around Chamonix, backpack in hand, traversing glaciers and ridges of the Mont-Blanc massif.
photos.learning_p2: That's where I met a guide who pulled out his camera between rope passages to capture grazing light on seracs. He taught me the essential: not to dominate the landscape, but to listen to it.
photos.learning_p3: The constraint of film — 36 exposures, no more — taught me patience and intention. Every shutter release was a decision, not a habit. My way of working has remained the same: few shots, lots of observation. Wait for the light, don't force it.
photos.territories_p1: Native of the Basque Coast, my first images were naturally of the ocean. Biarritz swells under grey autumn skies, villages perched on the foothills of the Pyrenees. I learned to read Atlantic light — soft, changing, sometimes brutal.
photos.territories_p2: Then in 2001, I arrived in Marseille. Everything changed. In a few hours of driving, you go from the turquoise blue of the Calanques to the ochre of the Luberon, wild Camargue marshes to Valensole lavender plateaus. A photographic wealth that never left me.
photos.territories_p3: The call of the open sea never stopped. Morocco first — Chefchaouen, Marrakech. Madeira next, vertical cliffs, laurel forests, levadas between two horizons. And always the Atlantic of my adolescence. No need to go to the end of the world — just observe what surrounds us.
photos.commitment_p1: For ten years, I've lived on Chemin de Morgiou, at the entrance to the Calanques National Park. This proximity transformed my perspective.
photos.commitment_p2: It was no longer just landscape photography: it was documentation, testimony. By diving in freediving, I discovered the extent of plastic pollution on the seafloor.
photos.commitment_p3: Photography taught me to see. Freediving taught me what there was to lose.
photos.passion_blockquote: No need to go to the end of the world — just observe what surrounds us.

underwater.editorial_label: Understanding my approach: from image to impact
underwater.editorial_p1: My photographic work revolves around three complementary axes forming a complete marine preservation cycle. Each section of this gallery addresses a specific need of the environmental photographer's approach.
underwater.editorial_p2_title: 1. Cleanup actions — The urgency of intervention
underwater.editorial_p2: Extracting a tire, a ghost net or batteries at 15 meters depth in freediving requires precise logistics. These images serve as visual evidence to alert public opinion and show that each waste removed is an immediate victory for the local ecosystem.
underwater.editorial_p3: We only protect well what we love, and we only love what we know. Despite proximity to urban areas, coralligenous communities, posidonia meadows, groupers and colorful nudibranchs struggle and thrive. These shots aim to recreate an emotional connection between the public and the sea.
underwater.editorial_p4_title: 3. Characterization — Transforming the image into scientific data
underwater.editorial_p4: By identifying the nature of materials, brands and state of degradation, we transform a citizen action into exploitable information. All data is reported on the ReMed Zéro Déchet Sauvage platform, feeding a national database for researchers and decision-makers.
underwater.editorial_p5: Beyond the technical or aesthetic framework, each dive, each shot and each reported data is an additional brick for the preservation of this common good. The goal remains the same: transform gaze into action and indignation into lasting solutions.
underwater.editorial2_h2: Freediving and committed photography — at the heart of Marseille's Calanques
underwater.editorial2_lead: A landscape photographer since adolescence, it was upon arriving in Marseille and discovering freediving ten years ago that my perspective shifted — from the horizon to the depths.
underwater.editorial2_method: I dive in freediving in Marseille's waters with a dual imperative: extract waste and document the agony as well as the beauty of the seabed. Unlike most underwater photographers who work with scuba, each image is taken in breath-hold, with cleanup equipment in hand, amid the waste, between 0 and 20 meters depth.
underwater.editorial2_impact: Each photo is a raw testimony — a visual shock to alert the public and convince institutions. This unfiltered gaze found an echo with ARTE, M6, France Télévisions and other media who relayed the fight for the Mediterranean.
underwater.editorial2_quote: "Photographing the seabed means making visible what no one wants to see."
underwater.editorial2_missions: This gallery brings together images from Team Oxygen and Opération Sentinelle missions, but also operations led alongside Boud'mer, Clean My Calanques, Mer Terre, Wings of the Ocean, Team AVA, 1 Déchet Par Jour, the Calanques National Park. From polluted depths to the resilience of wildlife — octopuses, spirographes, jellyfish, rocky seabeds — images that bear witness to both the urgency and the beauty of what remains to be protected.

arte.page_title: ARTE — Pollution: We Must Save Marseille & its Calanques
arte.hero_title: Pollution: We must save Marseille and its Calanques
arte.hero_subtitle: Full report on the Mediterranean and eco-actors' commitment.
arte.summary_title: Summary of the ARTE Regards report
arte.summary: Marseille, France's second city, but low in the ranking for waste management. Garbage that often ends up... at sea. Faced with the scale of the problem, residents decided to tackle it themselves. The Calanques are Karim's preferred terrain of action. When not at his finance controller desk, this fifty-year-old spends time underwater and on hiking trails. A freediver for years, he joined a local club three years ago. While he initially thought to admire the seafloor's beauty, he quickly confronts Coca Cola cans and thousands of debris. 'Cleanup' outings begin, very physical. With his GoPro, he documents dozens of kilos of objects brought up. His photos join those of the coastline, also polluted. His goal? Raise public awareness on social media and at exhibitions. Eric and Isabelle have made fighting waste their profession but with very different approaches. Behind his sunglasses, young Eric believes in festive mobilization. Armed with a megaphone, he works festivals and gathers hundreds of Marseillais for 'cleanup' operations where dance and good humor are always welcome. But the key for him is elsewhere. With the association he created, Clean My Calanques, he visits schools to convince children not to repeat the behaviors of their elders. As a complement to these methods, Isabelle chose science. When she arrived in Marseille in 2000, she was a young marine biology researcher. Dismayed by what she sees, she finds that wild waste is not then considered pollution. She dives into the subject, writes a thesis, and develops a characterization methodology to try to identify sources and responsible parties. A long journey for this ecologist, as for Eric and Karim. But together and thanks to hundreds of citizens who support them, they are determined. Marseille must be saved!
arte.quote_source: — Excerpt from ARTE Regards documentary commentary, broadcast in 2024
arte.editorial_subtitle: Marine environment documentary — Karim Saari in Marseille's Calanques
arte.editorial_p1: In 2024, European cultural channel ARTE devoted a report to Marseille eco-actors mobilized against plastic pollution in the Mediterranean.
arte.editorial_p2: At the heart of the documentary: Karim Saari, freediver and underwater photographer, committed within Team Oxygen and involved from the first edition of Projet Sentinelle. His freediving dives in the Calanques of Marseille — between 0 and 20 metres deep — document a raw reality: cans, nets, plastics and waste trapped in posidonia meadows. This European-scale broadcast gave increased visibility to cleanup missions and helped raise widespread awareness of the urgency of marine pollution in the Mediterranean.

greenGot.page_title: Green-Got — Mediterranean Short Film | Karim Saari
greenGot.hero_title: Under the Mediterranean, we filmed what postcards don't show
greenGot.hero_subtitle: An entire dump on the seafloor of a harbor divers believed pristine. Documented in freediving off Marseille for the Green-Got Foundation.
greenGot.film_p1: Chairs, tables, tarpaulins. An entire dump on the seafloor of a harbor divers believed pristine. This is what we documented in freediving off Marseille, for this documentary short film produced by the Green-Got Foundation.
greenGot.film_p2: The Mediterranean Sea is the world's most polluted sea. A semi-enclosed sea, it takes nearly 90 years to renew its waters: everything that enters accumulates. And 80% of this plastic comes from land. Once fragmented, it becomes invisible — found today in blood, placenta, breast milk, and the human brain.
greenGot.film_p3: Plastic is a petroleum derivative. The same industrialists who produce it are financed by the same major banks. The Green-Got Foundation exists to finance what the market will never pay for: cleaning a river, documenting pollution, picking up a million cigarette butts. The necessary, with no possible financial return.
greenGot.film_p4: Thanks to the Green-Got community, thousands of citizens have already been raised awareness and new cleanup missions launched on French coastlines. Every Green-Got card used daily finances this fight.
greenGot.film_p5: The ocean is resilient. If we stop pollution now, tomorrow it will be able to repair itself.
greenGot.participant_karim_desc: Marseille underwater photographer and freediver. With Projet Sentinelle, his association has removed more than 5.7 tonnes of waste from the seafloor in four editions — without a boat, starting from shore.

oxygene.page_title: Oxygène — Documentary on Cleaning Up the Mediterranean | Karim Saari
oxygene.hero_label: Documentary · Transfuges & Zéké Films · Supported by CITEO
oxygene.hero_title: Oxygène — Beneath the Mediterranean, the Atlantis of Waste
oxygene.hero_subtitle: 52 minutes in freediving alongside Team Oxygen: Coralie, Jérémy, Astrid and Karim Saari bring up from the seafloor what the city would rather not see.
oxygene.synopsis_p1: Marseille likes to say it lives with the sea. But the sea also lives with what the city dumps into it. Beneath the rocks where sunbathers gather, in the calanques and under the Mucem's docks, another world exists: one of waste that never truly disappears.
oxygene.synopsis_p2: This is the reality revealed by Oxygène, a 52-minute documentary following freedivers Coralie, Jérémy, Astrid and myself, from the Team Oxygen association, during our 4th Projet Sentinelle. Directed by Roxane Perrot and Ugo Isoard (Zéké Films), produced by Transfuges and supported by CITEO.
oxygene.immersion_p1: The directors didn't dive themselves, but they lived a full week with us: dawn departures, hours at sea, short nights. Team Oxygen never dives the same spot twice — the Côte Bleue one morning, Les Goudes the next, the mouth of the Huveaune after that.
oxygene.immersion_p2: When weather blocked the crossing to Frioul, an improvised stop at the Mucem revealed one of the film's most polluted sites: "We brought up 500 beer bottles in a single session. A few months later, another operation removed over a tonne of waste."
oxygene.quote_karim: "Underwater pollution isn't decreasing here. It feels like an endless cycle."
oxygene.quote_karim_source: Karim Saari, president of Team Oxygen, freediver and photographer
oxygene.apnea_title: Freediving, an aesthetic and philosophical choice
oxygene.apnea_p1: The film rests on a strong idea: freediving lets you film the sea on its own terms, without technical artifice. There's a kind of exploratory freediving, free of any competitive instinct. Underwater, you descend in silence, carried only by your own physical ability.
oxygene.quote_jeremy: "Where my freediving begins is when I feel the need to breathe."
oxygene.quote_realisateurs: "The sea showed us its suffering. But it also showed us its resilience."
oxygene.quote_realisateurs_source: Ugo Isoard and Roxane Perrot, directors of the film
oxygene.sisyphe_title: The myth of Sisyphus, underwater edition
oxygene.sisyphe_p1: Hundreds of cans, glass, plastics, tires, scooters, Vauban barriers, and sometimes surprising finds: a shell recently discovered near the Corniche, 30 nitrous oxide canisters at Les Goudes.
oxygene.stat_tonnes: Tonnes of plastic dumped into the Mediterranean every year
oxygene.stat_bottles: Bottles per minute, the equivalent of that dumping
oxygene.stat_microplastics: Of world ocean surface, yet of the planet's microplastics
oxygene.sisyphe_p3: "Some areas need three to four cleanups a year, the pollution builds back so fast. When I dive at Corbière, I know what to expect — I could almost draw the map of the waste. The hardest part is diving back a few days after a major cleanup and already seeing dozens of cans on the seafloor. It's as if the sea barely breathes before being smothered again."
oxygene.citeo_p1: "To protect, you must love. And to love, you must know" explains Christine Leuthy, CITEO's Southern Regional Director, who led the project for two years. The film chooses emotion over moralizing, to reach people at the heart rather than through instructions.
oxygene.quote_christine: "To change behaviors, you have to hit people right in the gut and the heart."
oxygene.screenings_p1: After a tour through Paris, Brignoles, the FIFES festival in Cannes and Nausicaá (Boulogne-sur-Mer), the film came back "home" with a private screening on June 24, 2026 at the Grotte Cosquer Méditerranée in Marseille, bringing together elected officials, companies and partner associations. It now continues rolling out across towns, schools, associations and festivals.

meduses.hero_subtitle: Enchanting ARTE documentary on jellyfish proliferation — with images provided by Karim Saari, filmed in the Mediterranean.
meduses.director_info: Directed by Sébastien Lafont — France, 2024, 43 min
meduses.desc_p1: Are jellyfish on the verge of dominating the oceans? Giving voice to one of them, this enchanting documentary reveals the superpowers of these seemingly fragile creatures, which benefit from overfishing, pollution and climate change to proliferate.
meduses.desc_p2: They have no heart, brain or skeleton and are 90% water. Despite their apparent fragility, jellyfish have conquered all the world's seas over 650 million years of evolution. But for several decades, from the Mediterranean to Norwegian fjords and Namibian coasts, their proliferation is alarming. This 'jellyification' of seas and oceans threatens fisheries and aquaculture worldwide.
meduses.desc_p3: Extraordinary reproductive capacity, formidable venoms, immortality… Through the voice of Aurelia aurita, the common jellyfish, this documentary reviews the superpowers of its relatives and examines the reasons for their spectacular expansion.

meduses.editorial_p1: The documentary 'Jellyfish | Sovereigns of the Oceans' was posted on YouTube on November 18, 2025 by ARTE Évasion. Initially broadcast in 2024, this film directed by Sébastien Lafont explores jellyfish proliferation and the transformation of marine ecosystems. I provided several images filmed in the Mediterranean for this production, from my fieldwork.
meduses.editorial_p2: The jellyfish is not an anecdotal subject in my world: it is at the heart of the Dark Massilia visual identity. Symbol of adaptation and evolution, it represents both the fragility of marine balances and the ability of life to survive disruptions.
meduses.editorial_p3: Contributing to this documentary is part of my ongoing commitment: documenting the ocean, understanding its mutations and making visible the weak signals that announce its transformations.

sources.page_title: Scientific Data — Marine Pollution in the Mediterranean | Karim Saari
sources.editorial_lead: Our field action rests on solid scientific data. Each year, approximately 570,000 tonnes of plastic are dumped into the Mediterranean — or 33,800 bottles per minute.
sources.plastic_p: A semi-enclosed sea representing less than 1% of global ocean surface, the Mediterranean concentrates nearly 7% of marine microplastics. These plastics fragment into persistent micro- and nanoplastics integrated into the water column, sediments and food chains. The plastisphere — the microbial ecosystem colonizing floating debris — promotes the spread of pathogens and exotic species.
sources.invasive_p: More than 1,000 non-native species have been recorded in the Mediterranean, introduced mainly via maritime transport and the Suez Canal. Among them, Rugulopteryx okamurae colonizes rocky seafloors down to 30 metres depth, forming dense mats that smother local benthic habitats. Plastic pollution and biological invasions are linked: floating waste facilitates exotic organism transport, while climate warming increases their establishment capacity.
sources.blockquote: Faced with pollution, invasive species and climate change, documenting and alerting is no longer activism — it is an ecological necessity.

sources.section_p1: Every figure presented on this site — whether on plastic pollution, the plastisphere or invasive species such as Rugulopteryx okamurae — is based on verified scientific publications.
sources.section_p2: This page gathers the studies documenting the real state of Mediterranean ecosystems: macro- and microplastic concentrations, ecotoxicological impacts, exotic species introduction dynamics, benthic habitat changes and interactions with climate warming.
sources.section_p3: Sources cited come from peer-reviewed journals (Science, Nature, PNAS, Marine Pollution Bulletin, Frontiers in Marine Science), international bodies (WWF, UNEP, FAO, European Commission), and academic and institutional work specifically dedicated to the Mediterranean and the Marseille coastline.

community.faq_dive_q: Can I dive or freedive during missions?
community.faq_dive_a: No. For safety and insurance reasons, diving and freediving are strictly reserved for certified members of Team Oxygen. External volunteers intervene exclusively from the surface, by kayak or from the shore.
community.faq_nodiver_q: How to help concretely without being a diver?
community.faq_nodiver_a: There are several ways to contribute: provide a kayak or boat to access isolated areas, participate in waste sorting and characterization on land, handle transport of bags to recycling streams, or document the mission with photos and videos from shore.
community.faq_notify_q: How to be notified about the next mission?
community.faq_notify_a: Join the 'Friends of the Calanques' Facebook group and follow @karimsaari on Instagram: we announce all dates on these channels first. You can also contact us via the Contact page to be added to our mailing list.
community.faq_official_q: Is Team Oxygen an official organization?
community.faq_official_a: Yes. Team Oxygen is a loi 1901 nonprofit association, with Karim Saari as president. Dives are supervised by certified members covered by associative insurance. External volunteers only intervene on the surface or on land.
community.faq_remote_q: How to support the movement without being able to come physically?
community.faq_remote_a: Digital support counts as much as field presence: follow our accounts, share our posts and reels, comment, tag friends who care about the cause. Each share reaches new audiences. You can also support the association directly on team-oxygen.com.

localGuide.page_title: Google Local Guide Marseille — Level 10 | Karim Saari
localGuide.anniversary_desc: Email sent by Google celebrating 9 years of contributions on Google Maps.
localGuide.editorial_p1: My engagement with Google started more than 9 years ago, at a time when the platform was actively developing 360° mapping via Street View.
localGuide.editorial_p2: At the time, Google lent me a 360° camera to document hard-to-reach areas. I covered the Calanques of Marseille, a complex territory partially inaccessible to standard capture devices.
localGuide.editorial_p3: I obtained the Street View Trusted certification, recognition granted to contributors capable of producing immersive content conforming to Google's technical standards. Street View has since been fully integrated into Google Maps, but the logic remains the same: document the real terrain.
localGuide.streetview_desc: Street View Trusted program — certification now integrated into Google Maps
localGuide.editorial_p4: Nine years later, these contributions have generated more than 183 million views on Google Maps. This concretely means that millions of people have discovered the Calanques, National Park trails or coastal coves through my photos and reviews — before even visiting them. A reach I wouldn't have imagined when accepting the 360° camera at the start.
localGuide.editorial_p5: My approach is not limited to mapping. I also publish underwater decontamination actions, waste extracted at sea, waste observed on trails and natural spaces.
localGuide.editorial_p6: The goal is twofold: enhancing the territory and making its real environmental state visible.

carte.map_desc: Green points: landscape photography · Red points: Team Oxygen cleanup
carte.editorial_h2: Our environmental actions in the field
carte.editorial_subtitle: Mapping of cleanup spots and photographs of the Marseille coastline
carte.editorial_p1: Explore the interactive map of the Calanques of Marseille to La Ciotat, at the heart of the Calanques National Park. This mapping covers the entire Marseille coastline: Sormiou, Morgiou, En-Vau, Sugiton, Callelongue, Cap Croisette, Cassis and the Calanques of La Ciotat.
carte.editorial_p2: Each point on this map corresponds to a real intervention or a documentary photograph. Far from a simple hiking map, this tool highlights a structural contrast: the preserved beauty of the limestone massif and the areas where pollution accumulates, sometimes invisible from the shore but revealed by freediving.
carte.green_desc: landscape photographs documenting the raw beauty of the Mediterranean limestone massif: cliffs, coves, underwater caves and unique coastal reliefs.
carte.red_desc: marine cleanup actions conducted with Team Oxygen: plastics, abandoned nets and submerged waste removed from the Calanques seafloor.
carte.spots_h2: Calanques spots: from Marseille to La Ciotat
carte.spots_intro: The Calanques National Park stretches over more than 20 km of coastline, from Marseille to La Ciotat. Here are the main sectors documented on the map:
carte.spot_sormiou_desc: The two inhabited calanques of the massif. Sandy bay floor, dense posidonia, access by foot or boat. Areas regularly cleaned by Team Oxygen.
carte.spot_sugiton_desc: Accessible only on foot from Luminy (45 min). Turquoise waters, vertical cliffs, exceptional marine biodiversity. Area with regulated attendance.
carte.spot_envau_desc: Among the most beautiful calanques in France. White sandy floor, sheer limestone walls, crystal-clear water. Limited access in summer to preserve the ecosystem.
carte.spot_callelongue_desc: Southern gateway of Marseille. Starting point for many Team Oxygen missions. Rocky floors richly inhabited, recurring freediving dives.
carte.spot_frioul_desc: Four islands facing Marseille. Clear waters, protected posidonia, gorgonians. Priority surveillance area against illegal mooring and waste.
carte.spot_ciotat_desc: East of Cassis. Wild, little-visited calanques, floors rich in gorgonians and groupers. Diving and cleanup area in expansion.
carte.bio_h2: Calanques Biodiversity: a threatened ecosystem to protect
carte.bio_subtitle: The marine floors of the Calanques of Marseille are home to one of the richest biodiversities in the Mediterranean — and one of the most vulnerable.
carte.bio_p1: You find posidonia meadows, red gorgonians, dusky groupers, sars, barracudas and occasionally large cetaceans in offshore waters.
carte.bio_p2: This wealth is directly threatened by plastic pollution, anchors that tear up posidonia and abandoned nets. Team Oxygen interventions aim to document and physically remove these threats, mission after mission.

accesMassifs.page_title: Forest Massif Access — Calanques | Karim Saari
accesMassifs.h1: Access to Forest Massifs of Bouches-du-Rhône
accesMassifs.dfci_desc: Updated every morning — real-time status of all forest massifs in the department.
accesMassifs.context_h2: The most exposed department in metropolitan France
accesMassifs.context_p1: The Bouches-du-Rhône combines the most unfavorable conditions for fire risk: hot dry summers, the mistral wind that turns flames into a torrent, and garrigue and Aleppo pine vegetation that ignites at the slightest contact. As a result, this territory is recognized as the most fire-exposed department in metropolitan France.
accesMassifs.context_p2: The figures speak for themselves: around 250 fire outbreaks per year, burning approximately 1,900 hectares annually. And most troubling: nearly 90% of these fires are of human origin. A cigarette thrown from a window, a grinder spark, an improvised barbecue — each of these acts can trigger an irreversible catastrophe in minutes.
accesMassifs.context_p3: What I have documented for ten years — limestone cliffs from the trails, the unique light of the calanques, marine biodiversity through freediving, posidonia, groupers — can disappear forever in a few hours if fire reaches the slopes. The sea and the forest form a single ecosystem. Protecting one means protecting the other.
accesMassifs.stat1_label: fire outbreaks per year in Bouches-du-Rhône
accesMassifs.stat3_label: of fires are of human origin
accesMassifs.regulation_p1: Every year, by prefectural decree, access, presence and movement in the forest massifs of Bouches-du-Rhône are subject to specific regulations from June 1 to September 30 inclusive, defined by the prefectural order of April 22, 2025. The aim is clear: reduce fire risk, protect people and allow rescue services to intervene without obstruction.
accesMassifs.regulation_p2: Each morning, Météo France evaluates the risk level for each massif. Based on this level, the prefecture authorizes, restricts or prohibits access to the areas concerned. This decision is published before 6am and applies for the entire day.
accesMassifs.regulation_p3: The regulations also apply to works in and near the massifs: brush clearing, thermal engines, agricultural work. In case of very severe or extreme risk, even professionals must stop all activities that could produce a spark.
accesMassifs.sign_caption1: This red sign can be found at every entrance to the Calanques when fire risk is deemed too high. It carries a fine of €135 for non-compliance.
accesMassifs.sign_caption2: The closure decision is published every morning before 6am by the Bouches-du-Rhône prefecture, based on the day's Météo France forecasts. It can change from one day to the next, even in the middle of July.
accesMassifs.sign_caption3: The rule is simple: before heading out, check the map above or the website
accesMassifs.risk_levels_h3: The 5 risk levels and their consequences
accesMassifs.risk_faible_text: Free access. All activities are permitted in the massifs.
accesMassifs.risk_limite_text: Access permitted. Heightened vigilance advised — avoid any risky behavior (fire, cigarettes, barbecue).
accesMassifs.risk_modere_text: Access permitted with restrictions. Some works may be supervised or limited.
accesMassifs.risk_severe_text: Access restricted or prohibited depending on sector. The most exposed massifs may be closed.
accesMassifs.risk_extreme_text: Total closure of massifs. All works and outdoor activities prohibited in risk areas.
accesMassifs.prevention_intro: Behind this regulation, there is no desire to prohibit, but an ambition to preserve. Our Mediterranean forests are among the richest in biodiversity in Europe. The women and men who fight the flames every summer do so sometimes at the risk of their lives. Every visitor who follows the rules is a link in this protection chain.
accesMassifs.geste_smoking_text: Not in the massifs, not from a vehicle nearby. A cigarette butt can start a fire hours after being thrown.
accesMassifs.geste_fire_text: Even in picnic areas, any open flame is prohibited during risk periods. Gas stoves should also be avoided.
accesMassifs.geste_tools_text: Chainsaws, grinders, brush cutters — any spark-generating tool is prohibited during severe risk periods.
accesMassifs.geste_report_text: Call 18 (fire department) or 112 immediately. Do not try to extinguish alone and move away from the area quickly.
accesMassifs.faq_h2: Frequently asked questions about massif access
accesMassifs.faq_season_q: When are the forest massifs of Bouches-du-Rhône subject to access regulations?
accesMassifs.faq_season_a: From June 1 to September 30 inclusive, access, presence and movement in the forest massifs are subject to specific regulations defined by the prefectural order of April 22, 2025. Outside this period, access is free but vigilance remains essential year-round, especially during spring or autumn heat waves.
accesMassifs.faq_close_q: Can the Calanques of Marseille close due to fire risk?
accesMassifs.faq_close_a: Yes. The Calanques National Park, the Marseilleveyre massif and the Côte Bleue are subject to prefectural forest massif regulations. Each day, based on the risk level assessed by Météo France, the Bouches-du-Rhône prefecture can restrict or prohibit access to all or part of these areas. The official DFCI map is updated daily.
accesMassifs.faq_why_q: Why are the Bouches-du-Rhône particularly exposed to fire risk?
accesMassifs.faq_why_a: The Bouches-du-Rhône is the most fire-exposed department in metropolitan France. This vulnerability stems from a combination of factors: hot dry summers, the mistral wind that accelerates flame spread, highly flammable garrigue and pine vegetation, and a high density of population and tourist activity. There are approximately 250 fire outbreaks per year in the department, burning around 1,900 hectares annually, of which nearly 90% are of human origin.
accesMassifs.faq_forbidden_q: What behaviors are prohibited in the massifs during risk periods?
accesMassifs.faq_forbidden_a: During high-risk periods, it is forbidden to smoke, light a fire or barbecue, operate thermal engines, carry out brush clearing or any other work generating sparks. These prohibitions apply to both professionals and private individuals near forest massifs.
accesMassifs.faq_check_q: How to check if the Calanques are open before setting out?
accesMassifs.faq_check_a: The most reliable method is to consult the interactive DFCI Bouches-du-Rhône map (opendfci.fr/13) or the site risque-prevention-incendie.fr/13, both updated every morning. This page karimsaari.com/acces-massifs-calanques integrates the official map directly and displays real-time massif status.
accesMassifs.faq_team_q: Can Team Oxygen organize cleanup missions during massif closure periods?
accesMassifs.faq_team_a: No. Before each underwater cleanup mission in the Calanques, Team Oxygen systematically checks massif access status. In case of prefectural closure, land outings and water entries from the calanques are cancelled or postponed. Volunteer safety and regulatory compliance are non-negotiable.

yab.page_title: The French — Yann Arthus-Bertrand | Karim Saari
yab.subtitle: Team Oxygen honored in YAB's photographic project — Marseille, 2024.
yab.img_alt: Team Oxygen in Marseille — Portrait by Yann Arthus-Bertrand for the Les Français project (2024)
yab.p1: This portrait of Team Oxygen was photographed by Yann Arthus-Bertrand, a major figure in contemporary photography and a pioneer of the environmental gaze on our planet.
yab.p2: A landscape photographer since my teenage years, I grew up with his images. His work profoundly shaped my vision: telling the story of a territory, revealing its beauty, and above all showing its fragility. In that sense, he represents a true artistic mentor for me.
yab.p3: When the production team contacted me to participate in the shoot, the answer was immediate: take this photo with Team Oxygen. Because our commitment to the Mediterranean, our cleanup actions and our deep roots in Marseille directly resonate with the humanist and ecological approach he has championed for decades.
yab.p4: This photograph goes beyond a simple portrait. It symbolizes a transmission: that of a perspective, a standard of excellence and a commitment in the service of the oceans.

photographeEnv.def_a: An environmental photographer documents nature — landscapes, wildlife and ecosystems — to raise awareness of the threats it faces. In Marseille, Karim Saari freedives to photograph the Calanques and their seabed, bearing witness to plastic pollution in the Mediterranean and inspiring people to protect it.

photographeEnv.timeline_h2: From landscape photography to engaged photography
photographeEnv.timeline_subtitle: A journey in three acts — the mountains, the sea, the seabed.
photographeEnv.tl_0_title: From age 6 to 1996 on the Basque coast
photographeEnv.tl_0_text: Born in 1971, I arrived on the Basque coast in 1977 — Bayonne, Biarritz, Capbreton, the Dune du Pilat, that Atlantic that sculpts the landscape as much as the people. It was here that my relationship with water, raking light, and the horizon was established. As a teenager, summers took me to the Alps — and it was there that I discovered landscape photography and acquired my first film SLR.
photographeEnv.tl_1_title: Between the Pyrenees and the Atlantic
photographeEnv.tl_1_text: Four years in Toulouse, within reach of the Pyrenees on one side, the Basque coast on weekends. I continued photographing the landscapes I had always known — the ocean, the dunes, the Atlantic light — before the Mediterranean changed everything.
photographeEnv.tl_2_title: Provence, and the northern districts of Marseille
photographeEnv.tl_2_text: June 2001: I arrived in Provence. First in Aix-en-Provence, then in Marseille from 2006. I settled in the northern districts — in Sainte-Marthe, the historic Ricard family neighborhood, steeped in popular and industrial memory. This was my landscape photography period: I discovered another Marseille — the hills, the calanques seen from afar, the white light on limestone — and published on 500px, where my work exceeded 800,000 impressions.
photographeEnv.tl_2_alt: Marseille — Old Port, arch and Notre-Dame-de-la-Garde
photographeEnv.tl_3_title: Valensole — National Geographic Special Issue n°183 Provence
photographeEnv.tl_3_text: A shot of Valensole lavender fields selected and published in special issue n°183 on Provence by National Geographic. Recognition by one of the world's leading landscape photography references — and a turning point in confidence in the image as a storytelling tool.
photographeEnv.tl_3_alt: Valensole lavender field, Provence — landscape photography by Karim Saari published in National Geographic Provence special issue
photographeEnv.tl_4_title: Chemin de Morgiou, freediving and the seabed
photographeEnv.tl_4_text: In 2017, I moved to Chemin de Morgiou, in the southern districts — right by the Calanques. I discovered freediving. I dived into the seabed for the first time — and I understood that the urgency was not on the surface. Tires, ropes, ghost nets: a silence no one sees from the surface. Photography became an act of witness. I brought waste back up with one hand, the camera with the other.
photographeEnv.tl_4_alt: Calanque of Marseille from the sky — swimmer in turquoise waters
photographeEnv.tl_5_title: Creation of the 'Friends of the Calanques' group
photographeEnv.tl_5_text: In 2018, I created the Facebook group 'Friends of the Calanques of Marseille to Port-Cros'. What started as a space for photographic sharing quickly became an engaged community — thousands of coastal enthusiasts, a relay for raising awareness about the preservation of the Calanques and mobilizing around field actions.
photographeEnv.tl_5_alt: Group of Friends of the Calanques of Marseille to Port-Cros
photographeEnv.tl_6_title: Vallon des Auffes — my first cleanups in La Provence
photographeEnv.tl_6_text: One of my first freediving cleanups, at Vallon des Auffes — that emblematic small port in Marseille. The operation was led by Team AVA, which I participated in as a simple volunteer, with my Beuchat hunting board equipped with a crate to collect waste: we brought up tires, scrap metal and plastics accumulated below the surface. La Provence devoted an article to the action — a first encounter with the urgency hidden at the bottom of the water.
photographeEnv.tl_6_alt: La Provence article 2018 — Karim Saari's first freediving cleanups at Vallon des Auffes, Marseille
photographeEnv.tl_7_title: Carrousel at the Old Port — City of Marseille
photographeEnv.tl_7_text: The City of Marseille commissioned a photograph of the Canebière to celebrate its pedestrianization. The photo was printed in large format on a banner, Place Saint-Louis, on the facade of Espace Culture — a public recognition anchored in Marseille's identity.
photographeEnv.tl_7_alt: Karim Saari — large format banner Canebière, City of Marseille, Espace Culture Place Saint-Louis
photographeEnv.tl_7_badgeAlt: Coat of arms of the City of Marseille
photographeEnv.tl_8_title: Les Pirates du Plastique — the zero waste adventure
photographeEnv.tl_8_text: I joined 'Les Pirates du Plastique', a campaign initiated by the local associative network and coordinated by the Calanques National Park, with the support of the City of Marseille and the Aix-Marseille-Provence Metropolis. About thirty events to question our lifestyles, shake up habits and bring the public along on the zero waste adventure. My first collective field engagement — before even Team Oxygen.
photographeEnv.tl_8_alt: Les Pirates du Plastique — Calanques National Park zero waste campaign, Karim Saari
photographeEnv.tl_9_text: Before the first edition of Projet Sentinelle, I chained cleanup operations in a climate of urgency. Repeated garbage collectors' strikes left waste flooding toward the sea — people were then talking of ecocide. I intervened in the water, mainly alongside the Merveille association, with logistical support from several associations. An intense mobilization that prepared the ground for Team Oxygen.
photographeEnv.tl_9_alt: Karim Saari diver — TF1 report on garbage collectors' strike in Marseille and environmental fears
photographeEnv.tl_10_title: Côte Bleue — I joined Team Oxygen
photographeEnv.tl_10_text: Already engaged in the field for years alongside other associations, I joined Team Oxygen for the first edition of Projet Sentinelle, as a simple freediver. Eight days of mobilization along the Côte Bleue, from Martigues to l'Estaque, bringing up waste buried in the seabed.
photographeEnv.tl_10_alt: Projet Sentinelle 2022, 1st edition — freediving cleanup on the Côte Bleue, Team Oxygen Marseille
photographeEnv.tl_11_text: Second edition, heading to the Frioul Archipelago. Seven days of freediving and surface logistics: barquettes, ropes and plastics brought up from the coves. I became more involved in the organization and took on the vice-presidency of Team Oxygen.
photographeEnv.tl_11_alt: Projet Sentinelle 2023, 2nd edition — underwater cleanup in the Frioul Archipelago, Team Oxygen Marseille
photographeEnv.tl_12_title: Calanques National Park — at the heart of Port des Goudes
photographeEnv.tl_12_text: Third edition, right in the Calanques National Park. Nine days of operations, from Port des Goudes to the classified coves: tires, ghost nets and plastic waste extracted one by one, by freediving between 0 and 20 meters.
photographeEnv.tl_12_alt: Projet Sentinelle 2024 — freediving cleanup at Port des Goudes, Calanques National Park
photographeEnv.tl_12_linkLabel: The Fondation de la Mer article
photographeEnv.tl_13_title: Pollution: We Must Save Marseille and Its Calanques
photographeEnv.tl_13_text: Filming for ARTE of the documentary 'Pollution: We Must Save Marseille and Its Calanques'. I guided the crew through the seabed, camera and waste in hand, to show a wide audience the scale of hidden pollution beneath the surface of the Mediterranean.
photographeEnv.tl_13_alt: ARTE filming 'Pollution: We Must Save Marseille and Its Calanques' — Team Oxygen and Karim Saari cleaning up in the Calanques of Marseille
photographeEnv.tl_14_text: Yann Arthus-Bertrand set up his Photo Studio in Marseille for his project 'Les Français'. I was personally invited to pose — and I took the opportunity to invite all of Team Oxygen to join me, for a group photo in front of the famous photographer and filmmaker's lens. A strong recognition of the collective's commitment to the Mediterranean.
photographeEnv.tl_14_alt: Team Oxygen photographed by Yann Arthus-Bertrand — 'Les Français' project, Photo Studio Marseille December 2024
photographeEnv.tl_15_title: Rade de Marseille — the record edition and Oxygène filming
photographeEnv.tl_15_text: Fourth edition in the Rade de Marseille: seven days, an expanded team and a record amount of waste retrieved. It was also during this edition that the documentary Oxygène was filmed. I was elected president of Team Oxygen in January 2026.
photographeEnv.tl_15_alt: Projet Sentinelle 2025 — record edition in the Rade de Marseille, Team Oxygen, Oxygène filming
photographeEnv.tl_16_title: Running Minds — Kilian Jornet Foundation in the Calanques

photographeEnv.faq_0_q: What is marine and coastal environmental photography?
photographeEnv.faq_0_a: Marine environmental photography uses images to document the beauty of underwater ecosystems and coastal landscapes, while illustrating the often destructive impact of human activity on these environments. It is a committed art that aims to transform aesthetic contemplation into genuine awareness and a call to action. It is particularly vital for revealing the fragility of spaces under pressure like the Mediterranean Sea.
photographeEnv.faq_1_q: What is the role of a committed photographer in Mediterranean conservation?
photographeEnv.faq_1_a: The photographer acts as a direct witness and whistleblower in the face of ecological urgency. By documenting landscapes, seabeds and cleanup operations, they make the sometimes invisible impacts of human activity on the biosphere tangible. Their goal is to give a voice to fragile ecosystems, denounce pollution, and highlight hope-bearing initiatives to create a powerful emotional connection with the public.
photographeEnv.faq_2_q: Why is the Mediterranean Sea such a crucial photographic subject?
photographeEnv.faq_2_a: The Mediterranean is a sea with a unique destiny: cradle of many civilizations, it is today under immense pressure, bordered by 24 countries and 427 million inhabitants. Award-winning contemporary photographers, like Angel Fitor, dedicate their work to revealing the creatures and marine ecosystems of the Mediterranean to show the hidden, fragile threads linking our existence to that of this sea.
photographeEnv.faq_3_q: How does photography help fight marine pollution?
photographeEnv.faq_3_a: Images have the power to translate abstract statistics about pollution into memorable visual realities. Photographer Chris Jordan, for example, illustrated the tragedy of ocean plastic pollution by photographing birds with stomachs full of waste. By photographing cleanup actions, one documents not only the consequences of overconsumption, but also shows the resilience of nature and the active solutions deployed in the field.
photographeEnv.faq_4_q: Can photography really help protect natural and coastal spaces?
photographeEnv.faq_4_a: Absolutely. Historically, photography has proven the value of ecosystems and has played a decisive role in justifying the sanctuarization of territories and the creation of national parks. Today, pioneers like biologist Cristina Mittermeier use images specifically for ocean conservation. Regular photographic monitoring is also a valuable tool for assessing coastline evolution and raising awareness among elected officials about land use planning.
photographeEnv.faq_5_q: What ethical rules must be respected in underwater and environmental photography?
photographeEnv.faq_5_a: Ethics is paramount: the well-being of marine fauna and the preservation of its habitat must always take precedence over obtaining an image. The eco-responsible photographer must maintain a safe distance to avoid stressing animals, never use bait to attract them, and limit disruptive artificial lighting. It is essential to be honest by refusing any deceptive digital manipulation in order to maintain the credibility of the conservation message.
photographeEnv.faq_6_q: How to contact Karim Saari for a report or collaboration?

photographeEnv.faq_7_q: What do you call a photographer who photographs nature?
photographeEnv.faq_7_a: They are called an environmental, nature or wildlife photographer. When the work explicitly aims to defend ecosystems, the terms committed or ecological photographer are also used. In Marseille, Karim Saari follows this approach: documenting the Calanques and the Mediterranean to protect them.
photographeEnv.faq_8_q: What does an environmental photographer do?
photographeEnv.faq_8_a: The job involves photographing natural environments, wildlife and plants, along with the human damage that threatens them, in order to inform and raise awareness. It combines technical skills — field, underwater, freediving — with commitment, often serving associations, media or environmental protection institutions.
photographeEnv.faq_9_a: An ecological photographer puts their work at the service of environmental protection: their images expose pollution, celebrate biodiversity and support on-the-ground action. Karim Saari is one example in Marseille, where he documents the freediving cleanup missions of the Projet Sentinelle.
